analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts and makes it harder to sue doctors, hospitals, and drug prescribers for negligence.
analysis.headline: The Senate cut off debate on the bill with a 48-42 vote that fell short of the 60 needed to proceed, so no senator ever cast an up-or-down vote on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overridden state law nationwide for medical malpractice cases. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 per provider, cut lawyer fees on a sliding scale, imposed tight deadlines for suing, made punitive damages available only for deliberate wrongdoing, and let juries reduce awards by the insurance payments a patient already received. Its stated purpose was to lower malpractice insurance costs and reduce defensive medicine, thereby improving access to care. It never became law: a procedural vote to begin Senate debate got 48 yes votes but needed 60, and the bill died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers would gain the most: damage caps, shorter filing deadlines, limits on lawyer fees, and a near-prohibition on punitive damages all shrink what insurers pay out in claims. Supporters argued patients would benefit indirectly, through lower malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine lowering health care costs. The bill also protects prescribers of FDA-approved drugs and devices from being sued alongside manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages (pain, suffering, disfigurement, loss of companionship) at $250,000 from a provider or single institution and $500,000 total from multiple institutions, while leaving economic losses like medical bills and lost wages uncapped.
Sets a three-year limit (or one year from discovery) for filing a medical negligence claim and requires courts to sanction lawyers who file frivolous suits.
Restricts attorney contingency fees on a sliding scale — 40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of anything above $600,000 — so more of any award goes to the patient rather than the lawyer.

Requires expert witnesses to be credentialed health care professionals in the same specialty as the defendant, and lets juries consider insurance payments the patient already receives when setting damages.

Allows punitive damages only for malicious intent or deliberate disregard proven by clear and convincing evidence, capped at the greater of twice economic damages or $250,000, and shields providers from being named in product liability suits for prescribing FDA-approved drugs and devices.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by negligent medical care would bear the cost. The hardest-hit would be those with the worst injuries and the least lost income — children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents — because the $250,000 cap applies to pain and suffering regardless of severity, and the collateral-source rule would cut awards by the value of insurance the patient already paid for. State courts and juries would also lose authority, since federal rules would preempt state tort law.

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages hits the most severely injured hardest — a child, a retiree, or a stay-at-home parent who has no lost earnings to claim can lose most of their compensation no matter how serious the malpractice.

The bill requires courts to reduce damages by the amount of any insurance or benefits the patient is already entitled to, letting a negligent provider's insurer off the hook for costs that the patient or the patient's health insurer already paid for.

Punitive damages would be available only for malicious intent or deliberate disregard proven by clear and convincing evidence, and the bill would bar naming a health care provider in a product liability suit over an FDA-approved drug or device — removing one path for holding prescribers and dispensers accountable.
The bill preempts state tort law nationwide — overriding state legislatures and courts that have already set their own rules on damages, expert witnesses, and joint liability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goals — steadier malpractice premiums and less defensive medicine — were plausible in principle, but the design tilted the cost onto the people least able to bear it. A $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages falls hardest on those with the worst injuries and no lost wages: children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents, for whom the cap is effectively the entire award. The collateral-source rule would let malpractice premiums already paid by patients be counted twice — once to the insurer, once against the verdict. The narrow conditions for punitive damages and the bar on naming providers in drug and device suits reduce accountability for negligent care, even as the bill leaves economic damages fully recoverable. On the whole, the financial gains flow to insurers and providers while the risks flow to injured patients, and the Senate agreed with the bill's critics rather than its supporters.

outcome.mechanism: Supporters brought the bill straight to the Senate floor, but a procedural vote to even begin debating it got 48 yes votes — eight short of the 60 needed — so the bill died there without ever being debated or amended.

narrative.text: Ensign introduced S. 22 on May 3, 2006, and it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day.
On May 8, 2006, a motion to proceed to the bill failed a cloture vote 48-42, short of the 60 votes needed to begin debate; every Democrat who voted was opposed and 48 Republicans supported it.
The bill never received an up-or-down vote and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and their lawyers are better off: all existing rights to sue for medical negligence survived intact, with no caps on pain-and-suffering awards and no new filing deadlines. Insurers and providers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was almost perfectly partisan: all 48 yes votes came from Republicans (48 of 55 voting yes), and 39 of 44 voting Democrats voted no, with 3 Republicans also opposed.

industries.note: Damage caps, a shorter filing window, collateral-source reductions, and near-elimination of punitive damages would all cut what insurers must pay out in claims. That is the point of the bill: lower payouts mean lower premiums or higher profits.

Providers gain sharply reduced liability exposure and predictable damages, which supporters said would lower malpractice premiums and reduce defensive medicine. The trade-off is that patients injured by negligent care absorb more of their own losses.

The bill bars naming a provider in a product liability or class action over an FDA-approved drug or device, making doctors and hospitals harder to reach and narrowing the web of accountability around drugs and devices already on the market.

Caps on noneconomic damages shrink case values, mandatory sanctions deter marginal filings, and the sliding-scale fee cap limits what lawyers can take from large recoveries — the bill is built to make medical negligence cases less lucrative to bring.
